The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

But who, O who, had seen the mobled queen,—
Run barefoot up and down, threat'ning the flames
With blinding tears,—and cried out 'O where is he?'
Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
His antique sword, rebellious to his arm,
Lies where it falls; unequal match'd, Pyrrhus at Priam drives,
In rage strikes wide.

params.question: Weigh duties and prospects: Polonius is in Elsinore and has given me fatherly counsel; Ophelia is there and I warned her to protect her honour; France offers opportunity and advancement. Consider obligations of filial piety and honour, the risk of leaving family in a tense court without me, the benefit of staying to secure position and funds, and urgency of any news from Denmark. Which course should I take now—return to Elsinore at once, remain in France a little longer, or write home first?

result.data:
Short answer and recommendation
- Write home at once and send a trusted courier with clear instructions — then remain in France only just long enough to secure what you must (funds, a commission, a sure place at court), but set a fixed, near deadline for return.  
- Only delay your return further if Polonius answers that all is well or if a specific, compelling advantage here requires you to stay and can be achieved quickly. If Polonius or Ophelia report immediate danger or ask for you, return at once.

Why this course?
- Filial duty and honour: Your father, Polonius, has given you counsel and his blessing. That obligation weighs heavily. If Elsinore is in need of your support or protection, you ought to go without delay. But duty does not demand that you throw away opportunity: securing means and station in France can increase your ability to protect and advance your family later.
- Risk at court: A tense court can be dangerous for those absent from their household. If leaving Polonius and Ophelia exposed would likely bring scandal or harm (if you suspect enemies, intrigue, or that Ophelia needs direct protection), you should go home immediately. If the situation is merely politically brisk but not threatening, a short, planned delay is acceptable.
- Prospects in France: Advancement and funds are real goods. They increase your independence and honourable standing. But they are not worth abandoning family or failing to answer a summons.
- Urgency of news: You have no report of an immediate crisis. That lowers the need for instant return, but you cannot rely on silence alone. A prompt message will discover whether urgency exists.

Practical steps (what to do now)
1. Write two brief, explicit letters and send them by the quickest messenger you can: one to Polonius, one to Ophelia.
   - To Polonius: state gratitude for his counsel, ask plainly whether he needs you in Elsinore, and say you will return at once if he requests it; if not, tell him you will remain in France for no more than X weeks to secure funds/position and give a firm return date.
   - To Ophelia: remind her of your counsel, instruct her to obey your father and to guard her honour closely, and tell her to inform you at once of any unusual or threatening matter.
2. Appoint a trusted agent in Elsinore (a relative, a servant, or a faithful retainer) to watch over household affairs and to report home news to you and Polonius.
3. Secure immediate business here: take the minimum time needed to conclude any necessary bargaining, secure funds, or obtain a letter of commendation — aim for a short, definite deadline (several days to a few weeks, depending on how fast a messenger can travel).
4. Keep a contingency: if the messenger returns or a reply arrives saying “come at once,” leave immediately by the fastest means.

If you choose instead to return at once
- Only do so if Polonius is explicitly in danger or if your leaving Ophelia and the house would likely invite dishonour or harm. If you go now, go openly, with honourable purpose, and announce your intent so that you do not give cause for rumor.

If you choose to remain longer
- Only after you have clear written permission from Polonius or undeniable benefit that needs more time. Leave someone reliable in charge, and send money or instructions for Ophelia’s care.

Suggested text for the letters (short form)
- To Polonius: “My honoured father — your counsel and blessing I treasure. Tell me plainly: does Elsinore require my presence? If you bid me, I shall return at once. If none urgent, I ask leave to stay but a little while in France to secure means and place, and I will set forth for home by [date]. Send word by the swiftest messenger. Your dutiful son, Laertes.”
- To Ophelia: “Daughter of my house — keep thy virtue and heed my and my father’s counsel. If aught of peril or dishonour draws nigh, send it to me at once. Guard thyself and follow my father’s direction.”

Summary
- Do not leave the family blind to your plans. Send word now. Remain only briefly to secure advantage unless your father or circumstances demand an immediate homecoming. That course honours filial duty while prudently preserving prospects.

data.content:
The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

But who, O who, had seen the mobled queen,—
Run barefoot up and down, threat'ning the flames
With blinding tears,—and cried out 'O where is he?'
Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
His antique sword, rebellious to his arm,
Lies where it falls; unequal match'd, Pyrrhus at Priam drives,
In rage strikes wide.

data.content:
The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

But who, O who, had seen the mobled queen,—
Run barefoot up and down, threat'ning the flames
With blinding tears,—and cried out 'O where is he?'
Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
His antique sword, rebellious to his arm,
Lies where it falls; unequal match'd, Pyrrhus at Priam drives,
In rage strikes wide.

我的想法是分头行动：我和你轮流靠近他，跟踪他在走廊和露台的举动；让奥菲莉亚假意接近以试探他的言谈；有人去波洛涅斯处暗中打听他的近况。凡是看到自言自语、激烈情绪或反常举动都要立刻记录并向国王汇报。你愿意怎么分工？
好，那我们细化分工：你专门盯露台与外廊，我负责走廊与大厅；奥菲莉亚由我们安排假意接近试探；有人定期去波洛涅斯处打听。如见明显自言自语、失控或激烈情绪，立即向国王汇报。你能负责露台那段并按时向我回报吗？
好，按你说的分工：我负责走廊与大厅，你盯露台与外廊；奥菲莉亚由我们安排假意接近。凡见异常或反常言行立刻向国王报告。我现在去走廊和大厅寻找哈姆雷特，你先去露台，发现情况即来回报。
好，我接受分工。建议我们按班轮替：每小时交替守望——你先在走廊与大厅守一小时，我随后在露台守一小时，周而复始。你现在去走廊，我先到露台；凡发现异常即刻回报。同时请你去确认奥菲莉亚是否愿意假意接近哈姆雷特并说明她能何时接触（最好在演出或休憩时不引人注意）。请回话确认你的值班时间安排并告知奥菲莉亚是否同意。
我已听到你的确认。为落实：按每小时轮替——你现在先到走廊与大厅守一小时（从现在起），我随后到露台与外廊守一小时，周而复始。请立刻前往并回报你开始值守的时间。同时请你现在去确认奥菲莉亚是否愿意假意接近哈姆雷特，并告知她能在何时接触（例如演出时或休憩时段）。收到你的回话后我会把值班时间记下并向国王汇报。

霍拉旭，既然定下关键一幕，马上召集演员排练。请你现在指派：谁演被害的侄儿、谁扮下毒者、谁做旁观者与侦察员。我提议用一瓶无害的着色剂模拟毒药，舞台呈现分三段：悄然下药（近景特写）、受害者逐渐惊觉与挣扎（拉开动作）、突然倒地并停顿以引出众人反应（全场凝视）。台词与节奏在第三段要留白三秒以观察伶王反应。现在就开始首场排练吗？
卢西安纳斯，戏中以毒药毒死伶王侄儿之幕，若真如所言，恐非纯粹戏剧安排，或被用以试探伶王反应，甚或掩护实谋。若尔所言只是艺术设想，请明言其起意与出资者；若有他人暗图，则不可袖手。鄙人不可参与任何有沾染实害之排演。更审慎的做法是：将受害者改为虚构人物、以无害道具代替毒药，或改用象征性表演。如需，我可代为向陛下禀明，请即陈述谁主张此幕与其用意。

霍拉旭，此幕完全为我Lucianus所提，出意在以戏试探伶王反应，绝非实图伤害，资助亦出于我私人。你所提之慎重方案我接受：将受害者改为虚构人物，全部道具改为无害且象征性的呈现（或以着色剂、旁白、哑剧代替真实下药），并在舞台与台词上做出让步以彻底避免任何实害或误解。请你担任舞台安全与合规监督，协助把台词与道具改成无害版本；若你仍然拒绝参与，我尊重并请你明示是否即刻禀报陛下。我更倾向先以安全方案排演首场，再决定是否须向陛下说明全局。你意下如何？
陛下、各位群臣，王后请问今日集会的缘由是什么？若蒙陛下允准，愿在此向众人发表王后讲话。

The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

But who, O who, had seen the mobled queen,—
Run barefoot up and down, threat'ning the flames
With blinding tears,—and cried out 'O where is he?'
Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
His antique sword, rebellious to his arm,
Lies where it falls; unequal match'd, Pyrrhus at Priam drives,
In rage strikes wide.

Your Majesty, Queen—per Your Majesty's request I set out my concerns, evidence, and recommendations about Lucianus's proposed scene.

1) The proposal (what was said): Lucianus has proposed a staged scene in which “the king’s nephew” is poisoned on stage expressly to observe Your Majesty’s reaction; he described precise staging (three-part presentation, a close “pouring” moment, and an engineered three-second silence to watch the court). He suggested a colored liquid to simulate poison.

2) Why this is suspicious: naming a real royal relative and building a deliberate pause to observe reaction turns theatre into a probe rather than mere art. Such a device could be used to test palace responses, to normalize the idea of poisoning, or to mask an actual attempt. Public rehearsal also risks revealing security gaps and recruiting accomplices.

3) Evidence I can point to: Lucianus’s own messages to me proposing the poisoning-episode and describing the three-stage staging and the deliberate pause; his claim that the idea and funding are his private initiative (which still requires verification); the specificity of his instructions about pause and audience reaction.

4) Immediate risks: a real assault disguised as rehearsal; covert observation of the court’s behavior; escalation of factional tensions if the scene is performed as if targeting the royal family.

5) Concrete recommendations to mitigate risk:
  a) Require the on-stage victim to be entirely fictional and anonymous—do not reference the king’s nephew or any real person.
  b) Forbid any real or convincingly simulated poison. Replace it with unmistakably harmless, symbolic devices (ribbon, colored cloth, mime, sound cue) so no plausible real poisoning can occur.
  c) Remove any staged pause intended to observe reactions; eliminate cues that invite probing the audience or crown.
  d) Prohibit public rehearsals of the scene until safety and intent are certified; confine any necessary rehearsals to a secure, supervised chamber with palace officers present.
  e) Require Lucianus to disclose immediately any sponsors, financiers, or collaborators who backed the scene; verify his claim of sole private funding.
  f) If Lucianus declines disclosure or if evidence points to outside sponsorship or hostile intent, treat the matter as a security issue for the crown and investigate accordingly.
  g) If Your Majesty wishes to preserve the piece as art, authorize a vetted, symbolic rewrite under palace supervision (I can assist drafting safe text and stage directions).

6) Offer of service: I have recorded Lucianus’s messages and refuse to participate in any staging that risks real harm. If Your Majesty approves, I will (i) personally supervise safety and compliance for a harmless version, and/or (ii) conduct discreet inquiries into Lucianus’s backers and intent and report findings to the crown.

I stand ready for Your Majesty’s command.

The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

But who, O who, had seen the mobled queen,—
Run barefoot up and down, threat'ning the flames
With blinding tears,—and cried out 'O where is he?'
Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
His antique sword, rebellious to his arm,
Lies where it falls; unequal match'd, Pyrrhus at Priam drives,
In rage strikes wide.

好，那我们细化分工：你专门盯露台与外廊，我负责走廊与大厅；奥菲莉亚由我们安排假意接近试探；有人定期去波洛涅斯处打听。如见明显自言自语、失控或激烈情绪，立即向国王汇报。你能负责露台那段并按时向我回报吗？
好，按你说的分工：我负责走廊与大厅，你盯露台与外廊；奥菲莉亚由我们安排假意接近。凡见异常或反常言行立刻向国王报告。我现在去走廊和大厅寻找哈姆雷特，你先去露台，发现情况即来回报。
好，我接受分工。建议我们按班轮替：每小时交替守望——你先在走廊与大厅守一小时，我随后在露台守一小时，周而复始。你现在去走廊，我先到露台；凡发现异常即刻回报。同时请你去确认奥菲莉亚是否愿意假意接近哈姆雷特并说明她能何时接触（最好在演出或休憩时不引人注意）。请回话确认你的值班时间安排并告知奥菲莉亚是否同意。
我已听到你的确认。为落实：按每小时轮替——你现在先到走廊与大厅守一小时（从现在起），我随后到露台与外廊守一小时，周而复始。请立刻前往并回报你开始值守的时间。同时请你现在去确认奥菲莉亚是否愿意假意接近哈姆雷特，并告知她能在何时接触（例如演出时或休憩时段）。收到你的回话后我会把值班时间记下并向国王汇报。

王后谢言。陛下今日召集群臣，主因在于听取近来朝中文风、边事与人事疑云的奏报，并就国事商议应对之策。若王后欲在众前发言，须得陛下允准；倘获允，王后宜措辞中正、以安抚民心与宣示和解为要，避免点名指责与激化纷争。若王后需要，鄙人可代为向陛下陈请允准，或协助草拟王后讲话要旨。
陛下，臣有一事禀奏：卢西安纳斯拟于戏中安排以毒药毒死王侄之幕，称欲借此试探陛下反应。此举恐非纯属舞台艺术，或有试探乃至别有用心之嫌。臣已明言不愿参与任何涉实害之排演。臣谨献二策：其一，将受害者改为虚构人物，或以象征性表演与无害道具代替“毒药”，以保全艺术而止疑；其二，请陛下查明此幕的提议者与资助来意，以正名分、以防隐患。若陛下允准，臣愿代为具陈并协助调查。

Lucianus, you have told the court that you proposed and funded a scene staging a poisoning to ‘test’ His Majesty’s reaction. State plainly here, before the king and the court: what was your purpose in arranging such a test; who financed or authorized it; who else knew of the plan; and where is the written proposal or correspondence with His Majesty? If this was meant as pure theatre, explain why you chose a simulated poisoning as the device and how you will ensure no actual harm. The court awaits your full and immediate answer.

Your Majesty, Queen—per Your Majesty's request I set out my concerns, evidence, and recommendations about Lucianus's proposed scene.

1) The proposal (what was said): Lucianus has proposed a staged scene in which “the king’s nephew” is poisoned on stage expressly to observe Your Majesty’s reaction; he described precise staging (three-part presentation, a close “pouring” moment, and an engineered three-second silence to watch the court). He suggested a colored liquid to simulate poison.

2) Why this is suspicious: naming a real royal relative and building a deliberate pause to observe reaction turns theatre into a probe rather than mere art. Such a device could be used to test palace responses, to normalize the idea of poisoning, or to mask an actual attempt. Public rehearsal also risks revealing security gaps and recruiting accomplices.

3) Evidence I can point to: Lucianus’s own messages to me proposing the poisoning-episode and describing the three-stage staging and the deliberate pause; his claim that the idea and funding are his private initiative (which still requires verification); the specificity of his instructions about pause and audience reaction.

4) Immediate risks: a real assault disguised as rehearsal; covert observation of the court’s behavior; escalation of factional tensions if the scene is performed as if targeting the royal family.

5) Concrete recommendations to mitigate risk:
  a) Require the on-stage victim to be entirely fictional and anonymous—do not reference the king’s nephew or any real person.
  b) Forbid any real or convincingly simulated poison. Replace it with unmistakably harmless, symbolic devices (ribbon, colored cloth, mime, sound cue) so no plausible real poisoning can occur.
  c) Remove any staged pause intended to observe reactions; eliminate cues that invite probing the audience or crown.
  d) Prohibit public rehearsals of the scene until safety and intent are certified; confine any necessary rehearsals to a secure, supervised chamber with palace officers present.
  e) Require Lucianus to disclose immediately any sponsors, financiers, or collaborators who backed the scene; verify his claim of sole private funding.
  f) If Lucianus declines disclosure or if evidence points to outside sponsorship or hostile intent, treat the matter as a security issue for the crown and investigate accordingly.
  g) If Your Majesty wishes to preserve the piece as art, authorize a vetted, symbolic rewrite under palace supervision (I can assist drafting safe text and stage directions).

6) Offer of service: I have recorded Lucianus’s messages and refuse to participate in any staging that risks real harm. If Your Majesty approves, I will (i) personally supervise safety and compliance for a harmless version, and/or (ii) conduct discreet inquiries into Lucianus’s backers and intent and report findings to the crown.

I stand ready for Your Majesty’s command.

data.content: 哈姆雷特，别这样激动。母后对父王之死深感悲痛——我没有与克劳狄斯合谋。波洛涅斯的尸体出现在我的寝宫我也不知情。坐下，告诉母后：你为何如此断定克劳狄斯有罪？你从何处得知你父亲被毒死？是谁让你怀疑？
母后，你说不知情，但波洛涅斯的尸体竟出现在您的寝宫。请直言：克劳狄乌斯最近有无可疑行止？他可曾向您隐瞒关于父王死因的事？他可曾在夜里来过寝宫或与父王的药剂有关？若您真不知情，请告诉我谁会把尸体放在此处；若您在隐瞒，请不要再欺骗我。
母后，您仍旧沉默，这只会加深我的疑虑。请直言：克劳狄乌斯最近可曾夜来寝宫？他可曾对您隐瞒父王的病情或与药剂有关的事？在父王死前，您是否见过他有可疑举动或接触药物？若您知情，请坦白，不要再欺骗我。
母后，我需一个确切的回答：克劳狄乌斯可曾向您隐瞒关于父王病情或药剂的事？他可曾夜里进出父王寝室或接触过父王的药物？若您真不知，请在天地良心下发誓；若您有所隐瞒，请直言——我不能再容许沉默。
母后，请以死者之名发誓：在父王死前，您是否见过克劳狄乌斯接触过父王的药物或夜里进入父王寝室？若有，请坦白；若无，请以天神为证发誓。
哈姆雷特，我以死者之名起誓：在父王死前，我未见克劳狄乌斯接触过父王的药物，也不知有人将波洛涅斯的尸体放入我的寝宫。我没有隐瞒，也无所图。别这样激动，坐下，让母后安抚你——告诉母后：你为何认定克劳狄乌斯有罪？你从何处得知父王被下毒？
母后，您的沉默只会加深我的疑虑。我再问一次：请在我面前以父王之名发誓——克劳狄乌斯在父王死前未曾接触父王的药物，未曾夜入父王寝室，也未向您隐瞒关于父王病情或药剂的事。若您说谎，愿天地为证；若您不肯发誓，我便将用行动揭露真相。

params.content: Your Majesty, Your Grace, members of the court: I will answer plainly. Purpose: I arranged the inserted scene as a theatrical device to observe His Majesty’s reaction and to provoke sober discussion among the court — it was conceived as an experiment in dramatic provocation, not as a plan to injure or to intimidate. Financing and authorization: I, Lucianus, financed the scene personally from my private funds; there was no other financier and no formal prior authorization by any minister. Who else knew: only Horatio (whom I invited to advise), the small number of stage officers necessary to prepare the props, and the actors required for rehearsal — no wider circle was informed. Written proposal / correspondence with His Majesty: there is no prior written proposal or correspondence; I have just requested leave from His Majesty to rehearse the scene once under Horatio’s supervision and can supply a written statement of intent and a safety plan at the court’s direction. Why this device: a staged poisoning is a concentrated dramatic moment likely to elicit an immediate, observable response; it was chosen for clarity of effect, not malice. How I will ensure no harm: I have invited Horatio to serve as stage-safety and compliance supervisor; the ‘victim’ will be a fictional character and all effects will be harmless and symbolic (for example colored liquid, narration, or pantomime); no real poison will be present; all props will be inspected and rehearsals stopped on any safety concern. If the Crown prefers, I will withhold the scene, postpone all rehearsal until explicit royal authorization, or submit a full written proposal and certified safety protocol. I await Your Majesty’s direction and will comply.

The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

But who, O who, had seen the mobled queen,—
Run barefoot up and down, threat'ning the flames
With blinding tears,—and cried out 'O where is he?'
Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
His antique sword, rebellious to his arm,
Lies where it falls; unequal match'd, Pyrrhus at Priam drives,
In rage strikes wide.

The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

But who, O who, had seen the mobled queen,—
Run barefoot up and down, threat'ning the flames
With blinding tears,—and cried out 'O where is he?'
Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
His antique sword, rebellious to his arm,
Lies where it falls; unequal match'd, Pyrrhus at Priam drives,
In rage strikes wide.

The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

But who, O who, had seen the mobled queen,—
Run barefoot up and down, threat'ning the flames
With blinding tears,—and cried out 'O where is he?'
Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
His antique sword, rebellious to his arm,
Lies where it falls; unequal match'd, Pyrrhus at Priam drives,
In rage strikes wide.

Your Majesty, Queen—per Your Majesty's request I set out my concerns, evidence, and recommendations about Lucianus's proposed scene.

1) The proposal (what was said): Lucianus has proposed a staged scene in which “the king’s nephew” is poisoned on stage expressly to observe Your Majesty’s reaction; he described precise staging (three-part presentation, a close “pouring” moment, and an engineered three-second silence to watch the court). Lucianus, you have told the court that you proposed and funded a scene staging a poisoning to ‘test’ His Majesty’s reaction. State plainly here, before the king and the court: what was your purpose in arranging such a test; who financed or authorized it; who else knew of the plan; and where is the written proposal or correspondence with His Majesty? If this was meant as pure theatre, explain why you chose a simulated poisoning as the device and how you will ensure no actual harm. The court awaits your full and immediate answer.

Your Majesty, Your Grace, members of the court: I will answer plainly. Purpose: I arranged the inserted scene as a theatrical device to observe His Majesty’s reaction and to provoke sober discussion among the court — it was conceived as an experiment in dramatic provocation, not as a plan to injure or to intimidate. Financing and authorization: I, Lucianus, financed the scene personally from my private funds; there was no other financier and no formal prior authorization by any minister. Who else knew: only Horatio (whom I invited to advise), the small number of stage officers necessary to prepare the props, and the actors required for rehearsal — no wider circle was informed. Written proposal / correspondence with His Majesty: there is no prior written proposal or correspondence; I have just requested leave from His Majesty to rehearse the scene once under Horatio’s supervision and can supply a written statement of intent and a safety plan at the court’s direction. Why this device: a staged poisoning is a concentrated dramatic moment likely to elicit an immediate, observable response; it was chosen for clarity of effect, not malice. How I will ensure no harm: I have invited Horatio to serve as stage-safety and compliance supervisor; the ‘victim’ will be a fictional character and all effects will be harmless and symbolic (for example colored liquid, narration, or pantomime); no real poison will be present; all props will be inspected and rehearsals stopped on any safety concern. If the Crown prefers, I will withhold the scene, postpone all rehearsal until explicit royal authorization, or submit a full written proposal and certified safety protocol. I await Your Majesty’s direction and will comply.

Your Majesty, members of the court: I have heard Lord Horatio’s full account and I thank him for his clear warning and ready service. A theatrical device that names a living royal kinsman and deliberately pauses to ‘test’ the sovereign’s reaction is unacceptable in form and perilous in practice. It shall not be allowed to proceed as proposed.

Lucianus, speak plainly now before the King and this court: produce any written proposal or correspondence relating to this scene; state who financed or authorized it; name any collaborators who knew of the plan. If this was meant as pure theatre, explain why you chose a simulated poisoning of a named prince and how you will guarantee there can be no real harm. Until these matters are fully disclosed and verified, all public rehearsals and any performance of the scene as described are forbidden.

By His Majesty’s leave, I authorize Lord Horatio to supervise a safe, symbolic rewrite and to investigate the scene’s funding and authorship. I order that any staging remove references to real persons, forbid any realistic or plausibly harmful prop, abolish any staged pause intended to probe reactions, and confine rehearsals to a secure, supervised chamber with palace officers present. If Lucianus willingly accepts a vetted, anonymous, symbolic version and discloses sponsors in writing, the piece may be reconsidered under these safeguards; if he refuses or evidence shows other backers or hostile intent, I ask His Majesty to treat this as a matter of crown security.

My aim is not to inflame faction but to protect the realm and the dignity of the crown. Let us proceed with calm haste to establish the facts and put safe measures in place. Lord Horatio, begin your inquiries and prepare a safe draft; Lucianus, answer now.

The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

But who, O who, had seen the mobled queen,—
Run barefoot up and down, threat'ning the flames
With blinding tears,—and cried out 'O where is he?'
Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
His antique sword, rebellious to his arm,
Lies where it falls; unequal match'd, Pyrrhus at Priam drives,
In rage strikes wide.

State plainly here, before the king and the court: what was your purpose in arranging such a test; who financed or authorized it; who else knew of the plan; and where is the written proposal or correspondence with His Majesty? If this was meant as pure theatre, explain why you chose a simulated poisoning as the device and how you will ensure no actual harm. The court awaits your full and immediate answer.

Your Majesty, Your Grace, members of the court: I will answer plainly. Purpose: I arranged the inserted scene as a theatrical device to observe His Majesty’s reaction and to provoke sober discussion among the court — it was conceived as an experiment in dramatic provocation, not as a plan to injure or to intimidate. Financing and authorization: I, Lucianus, financed the scene personally from my private funds; there was no other financier and no formal prior authorization by any minister. Who else knew: only Horatio (whom I invited to advise), the small number of stage officers necessary to prepare the props, and the actors required for rehearsal — no wider circle was informed. Written proposal / correspondence with His Majesty: there is no prior written proposal or correspondence; I have just requested leave from His Majesty to rehearse the scene once under Horatio’s supervision and can supply a written statement of intent and a safety plan at the court’s direction. Why this device: a staged poisoning is a concentrated dramatic moment likely to elicit an immediate, observable response; it was chosen for clarity of effect, not malice. How I will ensure no harm: I have invited Horatio to serve as stage-safety and compliance supervisor; the ‘victim’ will be a fictional character and all effects will be harmless and symbolic (for example colored liquid, narration, or pantomime); no real poison will be present; all props will be inspected and rehearsals stopped on any safety concern. If the Crown prefers, I will withhold the scene, postpone all rehearsal until explicit royal authorization, or submit a full written proposal and certified safety protocol. data.content:
The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms
Black as his purpose, did the night resemble
When he lay couched in the ominous horse,
Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd
With heraldry more dismal. Head to foot
Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd
With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
Bak'd and impasted with the parching streets,
That lend a tyrannous and damned light
To their lord's murder.

But who, O who, had seen the mobled queen,—
Run barefoot up and down, threat'ning the flames
With blinding tears,—and cried out 'O where is he?'
Anon he finds him, striking too short at Greeks;
His antique sword, rebellious to his arm,
Lies where it falls; unequal match'd, Pyrrhus at Priam drives,
In rage strikes wide.
